speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether children who are eligible for COVID-19 vaccination but whose parents do not approve of their vaccination, have their medical bills covered by the Government if they contract COVID-19; and (b) whether unvaccinated children have to be subjected to vaccination-differentiated safe management measures in schools and shared spaces in public.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: asked the Minister for Health whether the Ministry is continuing with its efforts to engage Singaporeans and Permanent Residents who refuse to be vaccinated and to educate them on the benefits of vaccination.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether he can provide an update on the COVID-19 vaccination rate of those eligible for vaccination aged 18 and below; and (b) whether COVID-19 vaccination will be made a requirement for participation in group activities in schools and educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: asked the Minister for Health in view of the emergence of the COVID-19 Omicron variant globally and subsequent tightening of border measures, what are the key quantitative or qualitative metrics and thresholds that the Government will consider before making a decision for domestic reopening plans to be rolled back and safe management measures tightened.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what is the Ministry’s strategy in containing the spread of the Omicron variant of COVID-19; (b) what measures should Singaporeans expect to be taken; and (c) how will these measures differ from previous measures implemented to contain the spread of the Delta variant or COVID-19 virus generally.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether there are plans to offer non-mRNA COVID-19 vaccines to children in the age groups of five to 11, and 12 to 18; and (b) if so, when can these vaccines be expected.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Health what is the impact from the emergence of the COVID-19 Omicron variant on the plans for Singapore to live with COVID-19 as an endemic disease, in terms of the timelines for reopening the economy and permitting more social and cultural activities involving the gatherings of people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Minister for Health whether the Ministry has plans to apply vaccination-differentiated measures to children aged between five and 11.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By working together, making collective sacrifices to restrain our social interactions, watching out for one another and implementing sound policies, we have overcomed perhaps the most difficult part of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most activities have resumed and we are meeting up with friends and loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our society has become much more resilient to COVID-19 than before.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But a new Omicron wave is upon us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we work together, we can ride through the wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once we have done so, we will be even more resilient than now and even more prepared to live with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When Omicron first burst onto the global scene, we immediately introduced measures, such as restricting travel from affected countries in Africa, enhancing testing for all travellers, isolating cases in hospitals and reinstating stringent contact tracing and quarantine for Omicron infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These measures will not stop Omicron from taking root and spreading in Singapore, given its high transmissibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, they have helped to delay its emergence, giving us precious time to understand it better and to prepare ourselves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The characteristics of Omicron have now become clearer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Cases are likely to double every two to three days.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, once cases start to rise steeply, within a couple of weeks, we may see 3,000 Omicron cases a day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, there has been consistent international evidence showing that Omicron infections are less severe than Delta.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, the clinical outcomes, particularly the number of people who become severely ill or die, are much more important than the top line number of infection cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This graph describes the situation in South Africa.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members can see three humps, reflecting the three waves that they have gone through: the first is Beta, then Delta in the middle, and the latest, the tallest is Omicron.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And it is plotted against the scale on the left axis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The grey part for the top graph shows hospitalisations, plotted against the scale on the right axis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, Members can see that in the latest wave, the number of hospitalisations is proportionately lower than the previous two waves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The red area shows number of deaths, plotted against a separate scale on the right axis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members can see that during the Omicron wave, the red area is actually very small; number of deaths is, proportionately, much lower than the previous two waves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next slide is a similar analysis but now, it is for the UK.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members can see a similar pattern, proportionately fewer hospitalisations and fewer deaths.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Among the patients admitted to hospital during the Omicron wave, they were 73% less likely to have severe disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the UK, the risk of being admitted to hospital or emergency care with Omicron was about half that of Delta.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Data from Denmark also showed that about 0.8% of Omicron cases were hospitalised, lower than the 1.2% rate of hospitalisation among cases infected with other variants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This has also been borne out by our own local experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In comparison, if these 4,322 infections had instead been caused by Delta, we would expect 50 to 60 patients needing oxygen supplementation, ICU care or to die.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, we should be careful in interpreting these observations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is early days and the circumstances of each country are different.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: South Africa, for example, has a young population and a high level of natural immunity, even though their vaccination coverage is low.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The UK has both high levels of vaccination and natural immunity, and this current Omicron outbreak is riding on the back of a protracted Delta outbreak, which worsens clinical outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, Omicron transmits much faster and infects more people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, even if a small percentage of infected individuals falls very sick, because of the large base of infections, it can still lead to many people needing ICU care or die.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The third thing we have found out about Omicron is that vaccines, especially boosters, retain substantial protection against severe disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, the most recent studies in the UK found that for vaccinated individuals, the risk of hospitalisation for Omicron is reduced by 72%, compared to the unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With a booster shot, vaccine effectiveness against hospitalisation is estimated to be 88%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Currently, Omicron has spread to over 130 countries and has become the dominant strain in many places.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, we lifted the suspension of flights from affected African countries and aligned the healthcare protocols between Omicron and other COVID-19 variants.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members would like to know our strategy in responding to the Omicron wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given that it is less severe than the Delta variant and vaccines still work against it, our key objective remains, which is, to live with COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, we can lead life as normally as possible and continue to build a bright future for Singapore and our children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That includes not locking down our borders, which will inflict tremendous pain on families, workers, businesses and also the mental well-being of many people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In any case, a severe lock-down strategy will likely delay but not prevent the inevitability of Omicron finding its way into our community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are two factors working in our favour.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, a high percentage of our population is vaccinated, and more are getting their boosters every day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, unlike many European countries which have to contend with a double whammy of a concurrent Delta and Omicron wave, we have only recently gone through a Delta wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are not likely to have to ride through two rapidly rising infection waves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In recent days, our overall local infection number is creeping up, to a few hundred a day, with Omicron accounting for about 40% of all cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given the transmissibility of Omicron, we expect the numbers to rise steeply in the coming weeks and Omicron will become the dominant variant within a few weeks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The responses that we have developed against Delta will continue to be relevant against Omicron, with some adjustments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In countries where Omicron has spread, the unvaccinated and under-vaccinated are still the most prone to falling seriously ill when infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Although the unvaccinated is a small proportion of our population, they contributed to 70% of the deaths in 2021.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The remaining 247 were vaccinated with a range of locally available vaccines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned, the sample size is small and they also do not account for other factors which may affect mortality, such as the age and timing of vaccination.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to try to convince those who are medically eligible to get vaccinated, through their primary care physicians, public messaging and the media.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, as Members would appreciate, as the number gets smaller, it is also harder and harder to convince them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those who are homebound, our Mobile Vaccination Teams can visit their homes to vaccinate them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the past months, we have managed to vaccinate well over 90% of every eligible age group.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are especially happy to see that among seniors aged 60 to 69, and 70 and above, 96% and 95% have been fully vaccinated respectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for those aged 12 to 19 years, 95% are fully vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the even younger ones aged five to 11, we have just started vaccinating them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The response has been good and operations smooth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At this time, only the Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty vaccine is authorised for use in ages below 18 years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to closely monitor the availability of other non-mRNA vaccines that are approved for use in children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the same time, our vaccine booster programme is gathering pace.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: About 46% of our population has received their boosters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have recently brought some 900,000 individuals aged 18 to 29 into the booster programme, of whom 700,000 are already eligible to receive their boosters today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As to whether there is a need for further booster shots – fourth shot, fifth shot – it is too early to tell.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, Israel is the only country that has authorised a fourth dose for non-immunocompromised individuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For an endemic infectious disease like influenza, we can draw some inference from there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This virus mutates frequently, so, people receive vaccinations every year to protect themselves against it, without many problems or the need for disruptive border closures and social restrictions each time there is an influenza infection wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a possible future scenario when we live with COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH and the Expert Committee on COVID-19 Vaccination (EC19V) will continue to monitor local and international data on the durability of protection from vaccine boosters and the evolution of the virus to assess the need for further vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second response: we continue to enhance our healthcare capacity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Particularly, for hospital ICU capacity, existing single rooms and isolation rooms can be repurposed into additional ICU beds when required.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Manpower is always a limiting factor, but ICU staff has increased by 12% over the past year to about 1,800 now and we have trained or are training about 500 more staff to assist with ICU operations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Anti-viral medications for COVID-19 have been used to treat vulnerable patients who are at high risk of falling severely ill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When authorised for use and made available in Singapore, these oral anti-viral medications will be important additions to the range of COVID-19 therapeutic agents already in use locally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have signed or are negotiating supply agreements for these medications but, unfortunately, I am not at liberty to release details due to confidentiality obligations in these contracts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Outside of the hospitals, we will be enhancing our health protocols to right-site patients, so that hospital resources go to those who need them most.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The MTF has recently announced our partnership with primary care doctors to care for patients who are recovering at home after being tested positive with Antigen Rapid Tests, under what we termed Protocol 2.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will help them safely recover and return to normal activities as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should caution Members against thinking that coping with a transmission wave successfully is a matter of recruiting more healthcare workers and building more ICU facilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our objective is not to have more people falling very sick and admitted to ICU but, in fact, to avoid it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, we size our emergency healthcare capacity based on what is sustainable and practical.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Bearing in mind this is a crisis of a generation, the capacity needed cannot be provided within our redundancy provision and ICU-trained staff do not just increase multi-fold overnight or even over a few months.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, we have tried to temper the infection numbers through safe management measures and exercising self-restraint in our social interactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, vaccinations, expansion of healthcare capacity and safe management measures, the three must work in tandem and we must strike a balance among the three factors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We cannot, for example, over-liberalise, remove all social restrictions, let infections rise uncontrollably and leave the healthcare system to bear the consequences.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Neither do we swing to the other extreme: protect the healthcare system at all costs, go for a zero-COVID-19 strategy and lock down our borders and society which will cause tremendous suffering to our people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How the three factors balance off one another is a matter of judgement, depending on the pandemic situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will be too rigid to set metrics and parameters to trigger social restrictions, as we need to respond flexibly and appropriately to the twists and turns that the pandemic situation may take.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This brings us to the third response, which is safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By restricting their social interactions, we protect them against infections and serious illnesses and taking up hospital resources.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is due to a combination of reasons, namely, children are less likely to develop severe illnesses when infected and we want to preserve as much as possible universal access to holistic education for children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in general, while we have a strict VDS system in place, to enable society to carry on normal lives as much as possible while protecting the unvaccinated, the rules are much less strict on children, based on the reasons I have explained earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members asked if we are likely to tighten up social activities because of the Omicron wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When the Delta wave subsided late last year, we refrained from being too jubilant and over relaxing restrictions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We kept our masking requirements, we did not allow night entertainment to restart, we kept group sizes at five.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is the MTF’s hope that we can ride through the Omicron wave with the current safe management measures posture.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we have to tighten the restrictions, it will be as a last resort and when our healthcare system is under severe pressure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Omicron is a different enemy, but we are much better prepared and much more resilient than before.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And after the Omicron wave passes, which it will, we would have taken another huge step towards living with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore will be one of the best and safest places to live in on Earth.
